John shows what true love is, namely, that which is referred to God as its first object. As previously John urged the effect, so now he urges the cause. For he wishes mutual love to be so cultivated among us, as that God should always be placed first [Calvin]. <div eID="gen40888" type="x-p"/>
entries.c18b76e120c36bff4fb281a3b1b42892b3a8c209: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18979"/><div sID="gen40889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18979"/><hi type="bold">3. this is--</hi>the love of God consists in this.<div eID="gen40889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not grievous--</hi>as so many think them. It is "the way of the transgressor" that "is hard." What makes them to the regenerate "not grievous," is faith which "overcometh the world" (<reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1Jo 5:4</reference>): in proportion as faith is strong, the grievousness of God's commandments to the rebellious flesh is overcome. The reason why believers feel any degree of irksomeness in God's commandments is, they do not realize fully by faith the privileges of their spiritual life. <div eID="gen40890" type="x-p"/>
entries.e298c4e508dcd3d4427ddbbe1e694b64bedb5c76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18980"/><div sID="gen40891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18980"/><hi type="bold">4. For--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1John.5.3">1Jo 5:3</reference>). The reason why "His commandments are not grievous." Though there is a conflict in keeping them, the sue for the whole body of the regenerate is victory over every opposing influence; meanwhile there is a present joy to each believer in keeping them which makes them "not grievous."<div eID="gen40891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whatsoever--</hi>Greek, "all that is begotten of God." The neuter expresses the universal whole, or aggregate of the regenerate, regarded as one collective body <reference osisRef="John.3.6">Joh 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.37">6:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.39">39</reference>, "where Bengel remarks, that in Jesus' discourses, what the Father has given Him is called, in the singular number and neuter gender, all whatsoever; those who come to the Son are described in the masculine gender and plural number, they all, or singular, every one. The Father has given, as it were, the whole mass to the Son, that all whom He gave may be one whole: that universal whole the Son singly evolves, in the execution of the divine plan."<div eID="gen40892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overcometh--</hi>habitually.<div eID="gen40893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the world--</hi>all that is opposed to keeping the commandments of God, or draws us off from God, in this world, including our corrupt flesh, on which the world's blandishments or threats act, as also including Satan, the prince of this world (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.30">14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.11">16:11</reference>).<div eID="gen40894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this is the victory that overcometh--</hi>Greek aorist, "... that hath (already) overcome the world": the victory (where faith is) hereby is implied as having been already obtained (<reference osisRef="1John.2.13">1Jo 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">4:4</reference>). <div eID="gen40895" type="x-p"/>
entries.998f4251375fa3a6f3a78c80ca7e891b4646036b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18981"/><div sID="gen40896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18981"/><hi type="bold">5. Who--</hi>"Who" else "but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God:" "the Christ" (<reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>)? Confirming, by a triumphant question defying all contradiction, as an undeniable fact, <reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1Jo 5:4</reference>, that the victory which overcomes the world is faith. For it is by believing: that we are made one with Jesus the Son of God, so that we partake of His victory over the world, and have dwelling in us One greater than he who is in the world (<reference osisRef="1John.4.4">1Jo 4:4</reference>). "Survey the whole world, and show me even one of whom it can be affirmed with truth that he overcomes the world, who is not a Christian, and endowed with this faith" [Episcopius in Alford]. <div eID="gen40896" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0a7d05ba40764d26ac6dd5c1724df2ad3fd6ce0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18982"/><div sID="gen40897" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18982"/><hi type="bold">6. This--</hi>the Person mentioned in <reference osisRef="1John.5.5">1Jo 5:5</reference>. This Jesus.<div eID="gen40897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that came by water and blood--</hi>"by water," when His ministry was inaugurated by baptism in the Jordan, and He received the Father's testimony to His Messiahship and divine Sonship. Compare <reference osisRef="1John.5.5">1Jo 5:5</reference>, "believeth that Jesus is the Son of God," with <reference osisRef="John.1.33">Joh 1:33</reference>, 34, "The Spirit ... remaining on Him ... I saw and bare record that this is the Son of God"; and <reference osisRef="1John.5.8">1Jo 5:8</reference>, below, "there are three that bear witness in earth, the Spirit, and the water, and the blood." Corresponding to this is the baptism of water and the Spirit which He has instituted as a standing seal and mean of initiatory incorporation with Him.<div eID="gen40898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and blood--</hi>He came by "the blood of His cross" (so "by" is used, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>: "by," that is, with, "His own blood He entered in once into the holy place"): a fact seen and so solemnly witnessed to by John. "These two past facts in the Lord's life are this abiding testimony to us, by virtue of the permanent application to us of their cleansing and atoning power."<div eID="gen40899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus Christ--</hi>not a mere appellation, but a solemn assertion of the Lord's Person and Messiahship.<div eID="gen40900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not by, &c.--</hi>Greek, "not IN the water only, but IN the water and IN (so oldest manuscripts add) the blood." As "by" implies the mean through, or with, which He came: so "in," the element in which He came. "The" implies that the water and the blood were sacred and well-known symbols. John Baptist came only baptizing with water, and therefore was not the Messiah. Jesus came first to undergo Himself the double baptism of water and blood, and then to baptize us with the Spirit-cleansing, of which water is the sacramental seal, and with His atoning blood, the efficacy of which, once for all shed, is perpetual in the Church; and therefore is the Messiah. It was His shed blood which first gave water baptism its spiritual significancy. We are baptized into His death: the grand point of union between us and Him, and, through Him, between us and God.<div eID="gen40901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is the Spirit, &c.--</hi>The Holy Spirit is an additional witness (compare <reference osisRef="1John.5.7">1Jo 5:7</reference>), besides the water and the blood, to Jesus' Sonship and Messiahship. The Spirit attested these truths at Jesus' baptism by descending on Him, and throughout His ministry by enabling Him to speak and do what man never before or since has spoken or, done; and "it is the Spirit that beareth witness" of Christ, now permanently in the Church: both in the inspired New Testament Scriptures, and in the hearts of believers, and in the spiritual reception of baptism and the Lord's Supper.<div eID="gen40902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because the Spirit is truth--</hi>It is His essential truth which gives His witness such infallible authority. <div eID="gen40903" type="x-p"/>
entries.da79e43403582b3de5676a8f6c5658eddeafa4fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18983"/><div sID="gen40904" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18983"/><hi type="bold">7. three--</hi>Two or three witnesses were required by law to constitute adequate testimony. The only Greek manuscripts in any form which support the words, "in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one; and there are three that bear witness in earth," are the Montfortianus of Dublin, copied evidently from the modern Latin Vulgate; the Ravianus, copied from the Complutensian Polyglot; a manuscript at Naples, with the words added in the Margin by a recent hand; Ottobonianus, 298, of the fifteenth century, the Greek of which is a mere translation of the accompanying Latin. All the old versions omit the words. The oldest manuscripts of the Vulgate omit them: the earliest Vulgate manuscript which has them being Wizanburgensis, 99, of the eighth century. A scholium quoted in Matthæi, shows that the words did not arise from fraud; for in the words, in all Greek manuscripts "there are three that bear record," as the Scholiast notices, the word "three" is masculine, because the three things (the Spirit, the water, and the blood) are SYMBOLS OF THE Trinity. To this Cyprian, 196, also refers, "Of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, it is written, 'And these three are one' (a unity)." There must be some mystical truth implied in using "three" (Greek) in the masculine, though the antecedents, "Spirit, water, and blood," are neuter. That THE Trinity was the truth meant is a natural inference: the triad specified pointing to a still Higher Trinity; as is plain also from <reference osisRef="1John.5.9">1Jo 5:9</reference>, "the witness of God," referring to the Trinity alluded to in the Spirit, water, and blood. It was therefore first written as a marginal comment to complete the sense of the text, and then, as early at least as the eighth century, was introduced into the text of the Latin Vulgate. The testimony, however, could only be borne on earth to men, not in heaven. The marginal comment, therefore, that inserted "in heaven," was inappropriate. It is on earth that the context evidently requires the witness of the three, the Spirit, the water, and the blood, to be borne: mystically setting forth the divine triune witnesses, the Father, the Spirit, and the Son. Luecke notices as internal evidence against the words, John never uses "the Father" and "the Word" as correlates, but, like other New Testament writers, associates "the Son" with "the Father," and always refers "the Word" to "God" as its correlate, not "the Father." Vigilius, at the end of the fifth century, is the first who quotes the disputed words as in the text; but no Greek manuscript earlier than the fifteenth is extant with them. The term "Trinity" occurs first in the third century in Tertullian [Against Praxeas, 3]. <div eID="gen40904" type="x-p"/>
entries.d04a09fea7f5a6bb30282e70d0cfd85ae6b4a0d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18984"/><div sID="gen40905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18984"/><hi type="bold">8. agree in one--</hi>"tend unto one result"; their agreeing testimony to Jesus' Sonship and Messiahship they give by the sacramental grace in the water of baptism, received by the penitent believer, by the atoning efficacy of His blood, and by the internal witness of His Spirit (<reference osisRef="1John.5.10">1Jo 5:10</reference>): answering to the testimony given to Jesus' Sonship and Messiahship by His baptism, His crucifixion, and the Spirit's manifestations in Him (see on <reference osisRef="1John.5.6">1Jo 5:6</reference>). It was by His coming by water (that is, His baptism in Jordan) that Jesus was solemnly inaugurated in office, and revealed Himself as Messiah; this must have been peculiarly important in John's estimation, who was first led to Christ by the testimony of the Baptist. By the baptism then received by Christ, and by His redeeming blood-shedding, and by that which the Spirit of God, whose witness is infallible, has effected, and still effects, by Him, the Spirit, the water, and the blood, unite, as the threefold witness, to verify His divine Messiahship [Neander]. <div eID="gen40905" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5107f962238285dc1a337c820fcf869ee01b7e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18985"/><div sID="gen40906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18985"/><hi type="bold">9. If, &c.--</hi>We do accept (and rightly so) the witness of veracious men, fallible though they be; much more ought we to accept the infallible witness of God (the Father). "The testimony of the Father is, as it were, the basis of the testimony of the Word and of the Holy Spirit; just as the testimony of the Spirit is, as it were, the basis of the testimony of the water and the blood" [Bengel].<div eID="gen40906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>This principle applies in the present case, FOR, &c.<div eID="gen40907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>in the oldest manuscripts, "because He hath given testimony concerning His Son." What that testimony is we find above in <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.5">5</reference>, "Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God"; and below in <reference osisRef="1John.5.10">1Jo 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.11">11</reference>. <div eID="gen40908" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3d2a2a0d2595b414f7e4e1cb95c34afb48b4961: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18986"/><div sID="gen40909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18986"/><hi type="bold">10. hath the witness--</hi>of God, by His Spirit (<reference osisRef="1John.5.8">1Jo 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen40909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in himself--</hi>God's Spirit dwelling in him and witnessing that "Jesus is the Lord," "the Christ," and "the Son of God" (<reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.5">5</reference>). The witness of the Spirit in the believer himself to his own sonship is not here expressed, but follows as a consequence of believing the witness of God to Jesus' divine Sonship.<div eID="gen40910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believeth not God--</hi>credits not His witness.<div eID="gen40911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made him a liar--</hi>a consequence which many who virtually, or even avowedly, do not believe, may well startle back from as fearful blasphemy and presumption (<reference osisRef="1John.1.10">1Jo 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen40912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believeth not the record--</hi>Greek, "believeth not IN the record, or witness." Refusal to credit God's testimony ("believeth not God") is involved in refusal to believe IN (to rest one's trust in) Jesus Christ, the object of God's record or testimony. "Divine "faith" is an assent unto something as credible upon the testimony of God. This is the highest kind of faith; because the object hath the highest credibility, because grounded upon the testimony of God, which is infallible" [Pearson, Exposition of the Creed]. "The authority on which we believe is divine; the doctrine which we follow is divine" [Leo].<div eID="gen40913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40914" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gave--</hi>Greek, "hath testified, and now testifies."<div eID="gen40914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>concerning. <div eID="gen40915" type="x-p"/>
entries.50c1dd90f1a781f82bfb87dda96ae1b6a2568db9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18987"/><div sID="gen40916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18987"/><hi type="bold">11. hath given--</hi>Greek, aorist: "gave" once for all. Not only "promised" it.<div eID="gen40916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">life is in his Son--</hi>essentially (<reference osisRef="John.1.4">Joh 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.25">11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6">14:6</reference>); bodily (<reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>); operatively (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2Ti 1:10</reference>) [Lange in Alford]. It is in the second Adam, the Son of God, that this life is secured to us, which, if left to depend on us, we should lose, like the first Adam. <div eID="gen40917" type="x-p"/>
entries.11ea8d0d26c6013cd70134de470548abd96ee3f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18988"/><div sID="gen40918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18988"/><hi type="bold">12. the Son ... life--</hi>Greek, "THE life." Bengel remarks, The verse has two clauses: in the former the Son is mentioned without the addition "of God," for believers know the Son: in the second clause the addition "of God" is made, that unbelievers may know thereby what a serious thing it is not to have Him. In the former clause "has" bears the emphasis; in the second, life. To have the Son is to be able to say as the bride, "I am my Beloved's, and my Beloved is mine" [So 6:3]. Faith is the mean whereby the regenerate HAVE Christ as a present possession, and in having Him have life in its germ and reality now, and shall have life in its fully developed manifestation hereafter. Eternal life here is: (1) initial, and is an earnest of that which is to follow; in the intermediate state (2) partial, belonging but to a part of a man, though that is his nobler part, the soul separated from the body; at and after the resurrection (3) perfectional. This life is not only natural, consisting of the union of the soul and the body (as that of the reprobate in eternal pain, which ought to be termed death eternal, not life), but also spiritual, the union of the soul to God, and supremely blessed for ever (for life is another term for happiness) [Pearson, Exposition of the Creed]. <div eID="gen40918" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5c34157dd342521628dc7ac31a01fff54758e75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18989"/><div sID="gen40919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18989"/>13. The oldest manuscripts and versions read, "These things have I written unto you [omitting 'that believe on the name of the Son of God'] that ye may know that ye have eternal life (compare <reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1Jo 5:11</reference>), THOSE (of you I mean) WHO believe (not as English Version reads, 'and that ye may believe') on the name of the Son of God." English Version, in the latter clause, will mean, "that ye may continue to believe," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="1John.5.12">1Jo 5:12</reference>).<div eID="gen40919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These things--</hi>This Epistle. He, towards the close of his Gospel (<reference osisRef="John.20.30">Joh 20:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.20.31">31</reference>), wrote similarly, stating his purpose in having written. In <reference osisRef="1John.1.4">1Jo 1:4</reference> he states the object of his writing this Epistle to be, "that your joy may be full." To "know that we have eternal life" is the sure way to "joy in God." <div eID="gen40920" type="x-p"/>
entries.d68612f11c87313c47ced6d77189b52cc44d7d7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18990"/><div sID="gen40921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18990"/><hi type="bold">14. the confidence--</hi>boldness (<reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1Jo 4:17</reference>) in prayer, which results from knowing that we have eternal life (<reference osisRef="1John.5.13">1Jo 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.19">1Jo 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.3.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen40921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to his will--</hi>which is the believer's will, and which is therefore no restraint to his prayers. In so far as God's will is not our will, we are not abiding in faith, and our prayers are not accepted. Alford well says, If we knew God's will thoroughly, and submitted to it heartily, it would be impossible for us to ask anything for the spirit or for the body which He should not perform; it is this ideal state which the apostle has in view. It is the Spirit who teaches us inwardly, and Himself in us asks according to the will of God. <div eID="gen40922" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a0813f8fbc84e82c06953bf7f3087b002d49495: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18991"/><div sID="gen40923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18991"/><hi type="bold">15. hear--</hi>Greek, "that He heareth us."<div eID="gen40923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we have the petitions that we desired of him--</hi>We have, as present possessions, everything whatsoever we desired (asked) from Him. Not one of our past prayers offered in faith, according to His will, is lost. Like Hannah, we can rejoice over them as granted even before the event; and can recognize the event when it comes to pass, as not from chance, but obtained by our past prayers. Compare also Jehoshaphat's believing confidence in the issue of his prayers, so much so that he appointed singers to praise the Lord beforehand. <div eID="gen40924" type="x-p"/>
entries.3be3895e6b8d08285a9521847f703d19cd2e0c6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18992"/><div sID="gen40925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18992"/><hi type="bold">16. If any ... see--</hi>on any particular occasion; Greek aorist.<div eID="gen40925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his brother--</hi>a fellow Christian.<div eID="gen40926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin a sin--</hi>in the act of sinning, and continuing in the sin: present.<div eID="gen40927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40928" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not unto death--</hi>provided that it is not unto death.<div eID="gen40928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall give--</hi>The asker shall be the means, by his intercessory prayer, of God giving life to the sinning brother. Kindly reproof ought to accompany his intercessions. Life was in process of being forfeited by the sinning brother when the believer's intercession obtained its restoration.<div eID="gen40929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40930" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for them--</hi>resuming the proviso put forth in the beginning of the verse. "Provided that the sin is not unto death." "Shall give life," I say, to, that is, obtain life "for (in the case of) them that sin not unto death."<div eID="gen40930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I do not say that he shall pray for it--</hi>The Greek for "pray" means a REQUEST as of one on an equality, or at least on terms of familiarity, with him from whom the favor is sought. "The Christian intercessor for his brethren, John declares, shall not assume the authority which would be implied in making request for a sinner who has sinned the sin unto death (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.35">1Sa 15:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.1">16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.3.29">Mr 3:29</reference>), that it might be forgiven him" [Trench, Greek Synonyms of the New Testament]. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.3.26">De 3:26</reference>. Greek "ask" implies the humble petition of an inferior; so that our Lord never uses it, but always uses (Greek) "request." Martha, from ignorance, once uses "ask" in His case (<reference osisRef="John.11.22">Joh 11:22</reference>). "Asking" for a brother sinning not unto death, is a humble petition in consonance with God's will. To "request" for a sin unto death [intercede, as it were, authoritatively for it, as though we were more merciful than God] would savor of presumption; prescribing to God in a matter which lies out of the bounds of our brotherly yearning (because one sinning unto death would thereby be demonstrated not to be, nor ever to have been, truly a brother, <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1Jo 2:19</reference>), how He shall inflict and withhold His righteous judgments. Jesus Himself intercedes, not for the world which hardens itself in unbelief, but for those given to Him out of the world. <div eID="gen40931" type="x-p"/>
entries.9220413f130ee3220fc4ebee2060614d02988411: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18993"/><div sID="gen40932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18993"/>17. "Every unrighteousness (even that of believers, compare <reference osisRef="1John.1.9">1Jo 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.4">3:4</reference>. Every coming short of right) is sin"; (but) not every sin is the sin unto death.<div eID="gen40932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and there is a sin not unto death--</hi>in the case of which, therefore, believers may intercede. Death and life stand in correlative opposition (<reference osisRef="1John.5.11-1John.5.13">1Jo 5:11-13</reference>). The sin unto death must be one tending "towards" (so the Greek), and so resulting in, death. Alford makes it to be an appreciable ACT of sin, namely, the denying Jesus to be the Christ, the Son of God (in contrast to confess this truth, <reference osisRef="1John.5.1">1Jo 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.1Jo">5), 1Jo</reference> 2:19, 22; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">5:10</reference>. Such wilful deniers of Christ are not to be received into one's house, or wished "God speed." Still, I think with Bengel, not merely the act, but also the state of apostasy accompanying the act, is included--a "state of soul in which faith, love, and hope, in short, the new life, is extinguished. The chief commandment is faith and love. Therefore, the chief sin is that by which faith and love are destroyed. In the former case is life; in the latter, death. As long as it is not evident (see on <reference osisRef="1John.5.16">1Jo 5:16</reference>, on 'see') that it is a sin unto death, it is lawful to pray. But when it is deliberate rejection of grace, and the man puts from him life thereby, how can others procure for him life?" Contrast <reference osisRef="Jas.5.14-Jas.5.18">Jas 5:14-18</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.12.31">Mt 12:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.32">32</reference> as to the wilful rejection of Christ, and resistance to the Holy Ghost's plain testimony to Him as the divine Messiah. Jesus, on the cross, pleaded only for those who KNEW NOT what they were doing in crucifying Him, not for those wilfully resisting grace and knowledge. If we pray for the impenitent, it must be with humble reference of the matter to God's will, not with the intercessory request which we should offer for a brother when erring. <div eID="gen40933" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ccd3d1cc2ab4bba0b8571d4d264b9518f8520ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18994"/><div sID="gen40934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18994"/>18. (<reference osisRef="1John.3.9">1Jo 3:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen40934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We know--</hi>Thrice repeated emphatically, to enforce the three truths which the words preface, as matters of the brethren's joint experimental knowledge. This <reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1Jo 5:18</reference> warns against abusing <reference osisRef="1John.5.16">1Jo 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.17">17</reference>, as warranting carnal security.<div eID="gen40935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whosoever--</hi>Greek, "every one who." Not only advanced believers, but every one who is born again, "sinneth not."<div eID="gen40936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that is begotten--</hi>Greek aorist, "has been (once for all in past time) begotten of God"; in the beginning of the verse it is perfect. "Is begotten," or "born," as a continuing state.<div eID="gen40937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keepeth himself--</hi>The Vulgate translates, "The having been begotten of God keepeth HIM" (so one of the oldest manuscripts reads): so Alford. Literally, "He having been begotten of God (nominative pendent), it (the divine generation implied in the nominative) keepeth him." So <reference osisRef="1John.3.9">1Jo 3:9</reference>, "His seed remaineth in him." Still, in English Version reading, God's working by His Spirit inwardly, and man's working under the power of that Spirit as a responsible agent, is what often occurs elsewhere. That God must keep us, if we are to keep ourselves from evil, is certain. Compare <reference osisRef="John.17.15">Joh 17:15</reference> especially with this verse.<div eID="gen40938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that wicked one toucheth him not--</hi>so as to hurt him. In so far as he realizes his regeneration-life, the prince of this world hath nothing in him to fasten his deadly temptations on, as in Christ's own case. His divine regeneration has severed once for all his connection with the prince of this world. <div eID="gen40939" type="x-p"/>
entries.fe6ff5bf9f8ba713ebee14a872486d57266bea22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18995"/><div sID="gen40940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18995"/><hi type="bold">19. world lieth in wickedness--</hi>rather, "lieth in the wicked one," as the Greek is translated in <reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1Jo 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.13">1Jo 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1John.4.4">1Jo 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.14">Joh 17:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.15">15</reference>. The world lieth in the power of, and abiding in, the wicked one, as the resting-place and lord of his slaves; compare "abideth in death," <reference osisRef="1John.3.14">1Jo 3:14</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1Jo 5:20</reference>, "we are in Him that is true." While the believer has been delivered out of his power, the whole world lieth helpless and motionless still in it, just as it was; including the wise, great, respectable, and all who are not by vital union in Christ. <div eID="gen40940" type="x-p"/>
entries.5137d77d31ce329ae08b5900b026905ec3b5503a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18996"/><div sID="gen40941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18996"/>20. Summary of our Christian privileges.<div eID="gen40941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is come--</hi>is present, having come. "He is here--all is full of Him--His incarnation, work, and abiding presence, is to us a living fact" [Alford].<div eID="gen40942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given us an understanding--</hi>Christ's, office is to give the inner spiritual understanding to discern the things of God.<div eID="gen40943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we may know--</hi>Some oldest manuscripts read, "(so) that we know."<div eID="gen40944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him that is true--</hi>God, as opposed to every kind of idol or false god (<reference osisRef="1John.5.21">1Jo 5:21</reference>). Jesus, by virtue of His oneness with God, is also "He that is true" (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Re 3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen40945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even--</hi>"we are in the true" God, by virtue of being "in His Son Jesus Christ."<div eID="gen40946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This is the true God--</hi>"This Jesus Christ (the last-named Person) is the true God" (identifying Him thus with the Father in His attribute, "the only true God," <reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>, primarily attributed to the Father).<div eID="gen40947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and eternal life--</hi>predicated of the Son of God; Alford wrongly says, He was the life, but not eternal life. The Father is indeed eternal life as its source, but the Son also is that eternal life manifested, as the very passage (<reference osisRef="1John.1.2">1Jo 1:2</reference>) which Alford quotes, proves against him. Compare also <reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1Jo 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.13">13</reference>. Plainly it is as the Mediator of ETERNAL LIFE to us that Christ is here contemplated. The Greek is, "The true God and eternal life is this" Jesus Christ, that is, In believing in Him we believe in the true God, and have eternal life. The Son is called "He that is TRUE," <reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Re 3:7</reference>, as here. This naturally prepares the way for warning against false gods (<reference osisRef="1John.5.21">1Jo 5:21</reference>). Jesus Christ is the only "express image of God's person" which is sanctioned, the only true visible manifestation of God. All other representations of God are forbidden as idols. Thus the Epistle closes as it began (<reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1Jo 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>). <div eID="gen40948" type="x-p"/>
entries.6293980308755cd3212d0b7c6ded4db49f5ff362: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18997"/><div sID="gen40949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18997"/>21. Affectionate parting caution.<div eID="gen40949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from idols--</hi>Christians were then everywhere surrounded by idolaters, with whom it was impossible to avoid intercourse. Hence the need of being on their guard against any even indirect compromise or act of communion with idolatry. Some at Pergamos, in the region whence John wrote, fell into the snare of eating things sacrificed to idols. The moment we cease to abide "in Him that is true (by abiding) in Jesus Christ," we become part of "the world that lieth in the wicked one," given up to spiritual, if not in all places literal, idolatry (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.5">Ep 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>). <chapter eID="1John.5"/><div eID="gen40950" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen40546" osisID="1John" type="book"/>

entries.f6d5e47eb94f1e7c8c82d1bba1591b9765554074: <div eID="gen55252" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen55253" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen55254" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen55254" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen55253" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen55255" type="x-p"/> He that believeth is born of God; loves God and his children; and keeps his commandments, which are not grievous, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.1-1Jn.5.3">1Jn 5:1-3</reference>. Faith in Christ overcomes the world, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.4">1Jn 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.5">1Jn 5:5</reference>. The three earthly and heavenly witnesses, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.6-1Jn.5.9">1Jn 5:6-9</reference>. He that believeth hath the witness in himself, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.10">1Jn 5:10</reference>. God has given unto us eternal life in his Son, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.11">1Jn 5:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.12">1Jn 5:12</reference>. The end for which St. John writes these things, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.13-1Jn.5.16">1Jn 5:13-16</reference>. The sin unto death, and the sin not unto death, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.16">1Jn 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.17">1Jn 5:17</reference>. He that is born of God sinneth not, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.18">1Jn 5:18</reference>. The whole world lieth in the wicked one, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.19">1Jn 5:19</reference>. Jesus is come to give us understanding, that we may know the true God, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.20">1Jn 5:20</reference>. All idolatry to be avoided, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.21">1Jn 5:21</reference>. <div eID="gen55255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55256" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen55256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55257" type="x-p"/> Whosoever believeth, etc. - Expressions of this kind are to be taken in connection with the subjects necessarily implied in them. He that believeth that Jesus is the Messiah, and confides in him for the remission of sins, is begotten of God; and they who are pardoned and begotten of God love him in return for his love, and love all those who are his children.
entries.54dee1637880a808bfdf8f59197fd14884f8a326: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen55257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55258" type="x-p"/> By this we know that we love the children of God - Our love of God's followers is a proof that we love God. Our love to God is the cause why we love his children, and our keeping the commandments of God is the proof that we love him.
entries.0c1b1b583b447e1399870a38dab0d71eabaee3c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen55258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55259" type="x-p"/> For this is the love of God - This the love of God necessarily produces. It is vain to pretend love to God while we live in opposition to his will. <div eID="gen55259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55260" type="x-p"/> His commandments - To love him with all our heart, and our neighbor as ourselves, are not grievous - are not burdensome; for no man is burdened with the duties which his own love imposes. The old proverb explains the meaning of the apostle's words, Love feels no loads. Love to God brings strength from God; through his love and his strength, all his commandments are not only easy and light, but pleasant and delightful. <div eID="gen55260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55261" type="x-p"/> On the love of God, as being the foundation of all religious worship, there is a good saying in Sohar Exod., fol. 23, col. 91: "Rabbi Jesa said, how necessary is it that a man should love the holy blessed God! For he can bring no other worship to God than love; and whoever loves him, and worships him from a principle of love, him the holy blessed God calls his beloved."
entries.e111ccf91b2eb3622abe46fa142124cb1fec8fd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen55261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55262" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever is born of God - Παν το γεγεννημενον· Whatsoever (the neuter for the masculine) is begotten of God: overcometh the world. "I understand by this," says Schoettgen, "the Jewish Church, or Judaism, which is often termed עולם הזה olam hazzeh, this world. The reasons which induce me to think so are, <div eID="gen55262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55263" type="x-p"/> 1. Because this κοσμος, world, denied that the Messiah was come; but the Gentiles did not oppose this principle. <div eID="gen55263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55264" type="x-p"/> 2. Because he proves the truth of the Christian religion against the Jews, reasoning according to the Jewish manner; whence it is evident that he contends, not against the Gentiles, but against the Jews. The sense therefore is, he who possesses the true Christian faith can easily convict the Jewish religion of falsity." <div eID="gen55264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55265" type="x-p"/> That is, He can show the vanity of their expectations, and the falsity of their glosses and prejudices. Suppose we understand by the world the evil principles and practices which are among men, and in the human heart; then the influence of God in the soul may be properly said to overcome this; and by faith in the Son of God a man is able to overcome all that is in the world, viz., the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, and the pride of life.
entries.f765f4118c9a301ac0f1a39394f15fc27d099ebb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen55265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55266" type="x-p"/> He that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God? - That he is the promised Messiah, that he came by a supernatural generation; and, although truly man, came not by man, but by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the Virgin Mary. The person who believes this has the privilege of applying to the Lord for the benefits of the incarnation and passion of Jesus Christ, and receives the blessings which the Jews cannot have, because they believe not the Divine mission of Christ.
entries.a392d5935c79d9658e2d06717a4f6ca92bbe8108: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen55266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55267" type="x-p"/> This is he that came by water and blood - Jesus was attested to be the Son of God and promised Messiah by water, i.e. his baptism, when the Spirit of God came down from heaven upon him, and the voice from heaven said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Jesus Christ came also by blood. He shed his blood for the sins of the world; and this was in accordance with all that the Jewish prophets had written concerning him. Here the apostle says that the Spirit witnesses this; that he came not by water only - being baptized, and baptizing men in his own name that they might be his followers and disciples; but by blood also - by his sacrificial death, without which the world could not be saved, and he could have had no disciples. As, therefore, the Spirit of God witnessed his being the Son of God at his baptism, and as the same Spirit in the prophets had witnessed that he should die a cruel, yet a sacrificial, death; he is said here to bear witness, because he is the Spirit of truth. <div eID="gen55267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55268" type="x-p"/> Perhaps St. John makes here a mental comparison between Christ, and Moses and Aaron; to both of whom he opposed our Lord, and shows his superior excellence. Moses came by water - all the Israelites were baptized unto him in the cloud and in the sea, and thus became his flock and his disciples; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.1">1Cor 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.2">1Cor 11:2</reference>. Aaron came by blood - he entered into the holy of holies with the blood of the victim, to make atonement for sin. Moses initiated the people into the covenant of God by bringing them under the cloud and through the water. Aaron confirmed that covenant by shedding the blood, sprinkling part of it upon them, and the rest before the Lord in the holy of holies. Moses came only by water, Aaron only by blood; and both came as types. But Christ came both by water and blood, not typically, but really; not by the authority of another, but by his own. Jesus initiates his followers into the Christian covenant by the baptism of water, and confirms and seals to them the blessings of the covenant by an application of the blood of the atonement; thus purging their consciences, and purifying their souls. <div eID="gen55268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55269" type="x-p"/> Thus, his religion is of infinitely greater efficacy than that in which Moses and Aaron were ministers. See Schoettgen. <div eID="gen55269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55270" type="x-p"/> It may be said, also, that the Spirit bears witness of Jesus by his testimony in the souls of genuine Christians, and by the spiritual gifts and miraculous powers with which he endowed the apostles and primitive believers. This is agreeable to what St. John says in his gospel, <reference osisRef="Joh.15.26">Joh 15:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.15.27">Joh 15:27</reference> : When the Comforter is come, the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me; and ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning. This place the apostle seems to have in his eye; and this would naturally lead him to speak concerning the three witnesses, the Spirit, the Water, and the Blood, <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.8">1Jn 5:8</reference>.
entries.6d1500e8eaa796a5c6ca33dbaab78ec9d003cc4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen55270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55271" type="x-p"/> There are three that bear record - The Father, who bears testimony to his Son; the Word or Λογος, Logos, who bears testimony to the Father; and the Holy Ghost, which bears testimony to the Father and the Son. And these three are one in essence, and agree in the one testimony, that Jesus came to die for, and give life to, the world. <div eID="gen55271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55272" type="x-p"/> But it is likely this verse is not genuine. It is wanting in every MS. of this epistle written before the invention of printing, one excepted, the Codex Montfortii, in Trinity College, Dublin: the others which omit this verse amount to one hundred and twelve. <div eID="gen55272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55273" type="x-p"/> It is wanting in both the Syriac, all the Arabic, Ethiopic, the Coptic, Sahidic, Armenian, Slavonian, etc., in a word, in all the ancient versions but the Vulgate; and even of this version many of the most ancient and correct MSS. have it not. It is wanting also in all the ancient Greek fathers; and in most even of the Latin. <div eID="gen55273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55274" type="x-p"/> The words, as they exist in all the Greek MSS. with the exception of the Codex Montfortii, are the following: - "<reference osisRef="1Jn.5.6">1Jn 5:6</reference>. This is he that came by water and blood, Jesus Christ; not by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit that beareth witness because the Spirit is truth. <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.7">1Jn 5:7</reference>. For there are three that bear witness, the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three agree in one. <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.9">1Jn 5:9</reference>. If we receive the witness of man, the witness of God is greater, etc." <div eID="gen55274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55275" type="x-p"/> The words that are omitted by all the MSS., the above excepted, and all the versions, the Vulgate excepted, are these: - [In heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one, and there are three which bear witness in earth]. <div eID="gen55275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55276" type="x-p"/> To make the whole more clear, that every reader may see what has been added, I shall set down these verses, with the inserted words in brackets. "<reference osisRef="1Jn.5.6">1Jn 5:6</reference>. And it is the Spirit that beareth witness, because the Spirit is truth. <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.7">1Jn 5:7</reference>. For there are three that bear record [in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one. <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.8">1Jn 5:8</reference>. And there are three that bear witness in earth],the Spirit, and the water, and the blood, and these three agree in one. <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.9">1Jn 5:9</reference>. If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater, etc." <div eID="gen55276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55277" type="x-p"/> Any man may see, on examining the words, that if those included in brackets, which are wanting in the MSS. and versions, be omitted, there is no want of connection; and as to the sense, it is complete and perfect without them; and, indeed much more so than with them. I shall conclude this part of the note by observing, with Dr. Dodd, "that there are some internal and accidental marks which may render the passage suspected; for the sense is complete, and indeed more clear and better preserved, without it. Besides, the Spirit is mentioned, both as a witness in heaven and on earth; so that the six witnesses are thereby reduced to five, and the equality of number, or antithesis between the witnesses in heaven and on earth, is quite taken away. Besides, what need of witnesses in heaven? No one there doubts that Jesus is the Messiah; and if it be said that Father, Son, and Spirit are witnesses on earth, then there are five witnesses on earth, and none in heaven; not to say that there is a little difficulty in interpreting how the Word or the Son can be a witness to himself." <div eID="gen55277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55278" type="x-p"/> It may be necessary to inquire how this verse stood in our earliest English Bibles. In Coverdale's Bible, printed about 1535, for it bears no date, the seventh verse is put in brackets thus: - <div eID="gen55278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55279" type="x-p"/> And it is the Sprete that beareth wytnes; for the Sprete is the truth. (For there are thre which beare recorde in heaven: the Father, the Woorde, and the Holy Ghost, and these thre are one.) And there are thre which beare record in earth: the Sprete, water, and bloude and these thre are one. If we receyve, etc. <div eID="gen55279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55280" type="x-p"/> Tindal was as critical as he was conscientious; and though he admitted the words into the text of the first edition of his New Testament printed in 1526, yet he distinguished them by a different letter, and put them in brackets, as Coverdale has done; and also the words in earth, which stand in <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.8">1Jn 5:8</reference>, without proper authority, and which being excluded make the text the same as in the MSS., etc. <div eID="gen55280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55281" type="x-p"/> Two editions of this version are now before me; one printed in English and Latin, quarto, with the following title: - <div eID="gen55281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55282" type="x-p"/> The New Testament, both in Englyshe and Laten, of Master Erasmus translation - and imprinted by William Powell - the yere of out Lorde M.CCCCC.XLVII. And the fyrste yere of the kynges (Edw. VI.) moste gratious reygne. <div eID="gen55282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55283" type="x-p"/> In this edition the text stands thus: - <div eID="gen55283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55284" type="x-p"/> And it is the Spirite that beareth wytnes, because the Spirite is truth (for there are thre whiche beare recorde in heaven, the Father, the Worde, and the Holy Ghost, and these thre are one.) For there are thre which beare recorde, (in earth), the Spirite, water, and blode, and these thre are one. If we receyve, etc. <div eID="gen55284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55285" type="x-p"/> The other printed in London "by William Tylle, 4to; without the Latin of Erasmus in M.CCCCC.XLIX. the thyrde yere of the reigne of our moost dreade Soverayne Lorde Kynge Edwarde the Syxte," has, with a small variety of spelling, the text in the same order, and the same words included in brackets as above. <div eID="gen55285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55286" type="x-p"/> The English Bible, with the book of Common Prayer, printed by Richard Cardmarden, at Rouen in Normandy, fol. 1566, exhibits the text faithfully, but in the following singular manner: - <div eID="gen55286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55287" type="x-p"/> And it is the Spyryte that beareth witnesse, because the Spyryte is truthe. (for there are three which beare recorde in heaven, the Father, the Woorde, and the Holy Ghost; and these Three are One) And three which beare recorde* (in earth) the Spirite, and water, and bloode; and these three are one. <div eID="gen55287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55288" type="x-p"/> The first English Bible which I have seen, where these distinctions were omitted, is that called The Bishops' Bible, printed by Jugge, fol. 1568. Since that time, all such distinctions have been generally disregarded. <div eID="gen55288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55289" type="x-p"/> Though a conscientious believer in the doctrine of the ever blessed, holy, and undivided Trinity, and in the proper and essential Divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, which doctrines I have defended by many, and even new, arguments in the course of this work, I cannot help doubting the authenticity of the text in question; and, for farther particulars, refer to the observations at the end of this chapter.
entries.81c9a9256f788c85199d490ca6d03072facc0605: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen55289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55290" type="x-p"/> The Spirit, and the water, and the blood - This verse is supposed to mean "the Spirit - in the word confirmed by miracles; the water - in baptism, wherein we are dedicated to the Son, (with the Father and the Holy Spirit), typifying his spotless purity, and the inward purifying of our nature; and the blood - represented in the Lord's Supper, and applied to the consciences of believers: and all these harmoniously agree in the same testimony, that Jesus Christ is the Divine, the complete, the only Savior of the world." - Mr. Wesley's notes. <div eID="gen55290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55291" type="x-p"/> By the written word, which proceeded from the Holy Spirit, that Spirit is continually witnessing upon earth, that God hath given unto us eternal life. <div eID="gen55291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55292" type="x-p"/> By baptism, which points out our regeneration, and the renewing of the Holy Ghost, and which is still maintained as an initiatory rite in the Christian Church, we have another witness on earth of the truth, certainty, importance, and efficacy of the Christian religion. The same may be said of the blood, represented by the holy eucharist, which continues to show forth the death and atoning sacrifice of the Son of God till he comes. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Jn.5.6">1Jn 5:6</reference>.
entries.a2e8174e183e78c6d674718ad8399ae0feafb4cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen55292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55293" type="x-p"/> If we receive the witness of men - Which all are obliged to do, and which is deemed a sufficient testimony to truth in numberless cases; the witness of God is greater - he can neither be deceived nor deceive, but man may deceive and be deceived.
entries.b7028526b00d90e6098cb09607a5bfc9a7ef7e84: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen55293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55294" type="x-p"/> He that believeth on the Son of God - This is God's witness to a truth, the most important and interesting to mankind. God has witnessed that whosoever believeth on his Son shall be saved, and have everlasting life; and shall have the witness of it in himself, the Spirit bearing witness with his spirit that he is a child of God. To know, to feel his sin forgiven, to have the testimony of this in the heart from the Holy Spirit himself, is the privilege of every true believer in Christ.
entries.6aa59b5cbf3442f7b447beeea327d83a9390e87c: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen55294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55295" type="x-p"/> This is the record - The great truth to which the Spirit, the water, and the blood bear testimony. God hath given us eternal life - a right to endless glory, and a meetness for it. And this life is in his Son; it comes by and through him; he is its author and its purchaser; it is only in and through Him. No other scheme of salvation can be effectual; God has provided none other, and in such a case a man's invention must be vain.
entries.3f0b2df3c2fc60e4332d07a730fd3fef876f56a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen55295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55296" type="x-p"/> He that hath the Son hath life - As the eternal life is given In the Son of God, it follows that it cannot be enjoyed without him. No man can have it without having Christ; therefore he that hath the Son hath life, and he that hath not the Son hath not life. It is in vain to expect eternal glory, if we have not Christ in our heart. The indwelling Christ gives both a title to it, and a meetness for it. This is God's record. Let no man deceive himself here. An indwelling Christ and Glory; no indwelling Christ, No glory. God's record must stand.
entries.541a151f20bb97e6670bdd7b9c0ea7f787d2ead0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen55296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55297" type="x-p"/> That ye may know that ye have eternal life - I write to show your privileges - to lead you into this holy of holies - to show what believing on the Son of God is, by the glorious effects it produces: it is not a blind reliance for, but an actual enjoyment of, salvation; Christ living, working, and reigning in the heart. <div eID="gen55297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55298" type="x-p"/> And that ye may believe - That is, continue to believe: for Christ dwells in the heart only by Faith, and faith lives only by Love, and love continues only by Obedience; he who Believes loves, and he who Loves obeys. He who obeys loves; he who loves believes; he who believes has the witness in himself: he who has this witness has Christ in his heart, the hope of glory; and he who believes, loves, and obeys, has Christ in his heart, and is a man of prayer.
entries.369cca40abbbd2e4f626277f91e156b3e477b635: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen55298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55299" type="x-p"/> This is the confidence - Παρῥησια, The liberty of access and speech, that if we ask any thing according to his will, that is, which he has promised in his word. His word is a revelation of his will, in the things which concern the salvation of man. All that God has promised we are justified in expecting; and what he has promised, and we expect, we should pray for. Prayer is the language of the children of God. He who is begotten of God speaks this language. He calls God Abba, Father, in the true spirit of supplication. Prayer is the language of dependence on God; where the soul is dumb, there is neither life, love, nor faith. Faith and prayer are not boldly to advance claims upon God; we must take heed that what we ask and believe for is agreeable to the revealed will of God. What we find promised, that we may plead.
entries.e87b9f27ffbcbe1e0ed1a9b3b20b7264f4f41918: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen55299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55300" type="x-p"/> And if we know that he hear us - Seeing we are satisfied that he hears the prayer of faith, requesting the things which himself has promised; we know, consequently, that we have the petitions - the answer to the petitions, that we desired of him; for he cannot deny himself; and we may consider them as sure as if we had them; and we shall have them as soon as we plead for and need them. We are not to ask to-day for mercy that we now need, and not receive it till to-morrow, or some future time. God gives it to him who prays, when it is needful.
entries.eb3779b68ae135fe51dd3ff97eb02b3eb667e82f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen55300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55301" type="x-p"/> A sin which is not unto death - This is an extremely difficult passage, and has been variously interpreted. What is the sin not unto death, for which we should ask, and life shall be given to him that commits it? And what is the sin unto death, for which we should not pray? <div eID="gen55301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55302" type="x-p"/> I shall note three of the chief opinions on this subject: - <div eID="gen55302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55303" type="x-p"/> 1. It is supposed that there is here an allusion to a distinction in the Jewish law, where there was חטאה למיתה chattaah lemithah, "a sin unto death;" and חטאה לא למיתה chattaah lo lemithah, "a sin not unto death;" that is, <div eID="gen55303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55304" type="x-p"/> 1. A sin, or transgression, to which the law had assigned the punishment of death; such as idolatry, incest, blasphemy, breach of the Sabbath, and the like. And <div eID="gen55304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55305" type="x-p"/> 2. A sin not unto death, i.e. transgressions of ignorance, inadvertence, etc., and such is, in their own nature, appear to be comparatively light and trivial. That such distinctions did exist in the Jewish synagogue both Schoettgen and Carpzovius have proved. <div eID="gen55305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55306" type="x-p"/> 2. By the sin not unto death, for which intercession might be made, and unto death, for which prayer might not be made, we are to understand transgressions of the civil law of a particular place, some of which must be punished with death, according to the statutes, the crime admitting of no pardon: others might be punished with death, but the magistrate had the power of commuting the punishments, i.e. of changing death into banishment, etc., for reasons that might appear to him satisfactory, or at the intercession of powerful friends. To intercede in the former case would be useless, because the law would not relax, therefore they need not pray for it; but intercession in the latter case might be prevalent, therefore they might pray; and if they did not, the person might suffer the punishment of death. This opinion, which has been advanced by Rosenmuller, intimates that men should feel for each other's distresses, and use their influence in behalf of the wretched, nor ever abandon the unfortunate but where the case is utterly hopeless. <div eID="gen55306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55307" type="x-p"/> 3. The sin unto death means a case of transgression, particularly of grievous backsliding from the life and power of godliness, which God determines to punish with temporal death, while at the same time he extends mercy to the penitent soul. The disobedient prophet, 1 Kings 13:1-32, is, on this interpretation, a case in point: many others occur in the history of the Church, and of every religious community. The sin not unto death is any sin which God does not choose thus to punish. This view of the subject is that taken by the late Rev. J. Wesley, in a sermon entitled, A Call to Backsliders. - Works, vol ii. page 239. <div eID="gen55307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55308" type="x-p"/> I do not think the passage has any thing to do with what is termed the sin against the Holy Ghost; much less with the popish doctrine of purgatory; nor with sins committed before and after baptism, the former pardonable, the latter unpardonable, according to some of the fathers. Either of the last opinions (viz., 2 and 3) make a good sense; and the first (1) is not unlikely: the apostle may allude to some maxim or custom in the Jewish Church which is not now distinctly known. However, this we know, that any penitent may find mercy through Christ Jesus; for through him every kind of sin may be forgiven to man, except the sin against the Holy Ghost; which I have proved no man can now commit. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.12.31">Mat 12:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.12.39">Mat 12:39</reference> (note).
entries.881850d0d57f6a058747cbd328d8cfdd94fc27aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen55308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55309" type="x-p"/> All unrighteousness is sin - Πασα αδικια, Every act contrary to justice is sin - is a transgression of the law which condemns all injustice.
entries.07747194fee2fe1af82cc91627f4386065b6d6a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen55309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55310" type="x-p"/> Whosoever is born of God sinneth not - This is spoken of adult Christians; they are cleansed from all unrighteousness, consequently from all sin, <reference osisRef="1Jn.1.7-1Jn.1.9">1Jn 1:7-9</reference>. <div eID="gen55310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55311" type="x-p"/> Keepeth himself - That is, in the love of God, <reference osisRef="Jde.1.21">Jde 1:21</reference>, by building up himself on his most holy faith, and praying in the Holy Ghost; and that wicked one - the devil, toucheth him not - finds nothing of his own nature in him on which he can work, Christ dwelling in his heart by faith.
entries.0c041a047455896ba005e715a35bd58aea372f3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen55311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55312" type="x-p"/> We know that we are of God - Have the fullest proof of the truth of Christianity, and of our own reconciliation to God through the death of his Son. <div eID="gen55312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55313" type="x-p"/> The whole world lieth in wickedness - Εν τῳ πονηρῳ κειται· Lieth in the wicked one - is embraced in the arms of the devil, where it lies fast asleep and carnally secure, deriving its heat and power from its infernal fosterer. What a truly awful state! And do not the actions, tempers, propensities, opinions and maxims of all worldly men prove and illustrate this? "In this short expression," says Mr. Wesley, "the horrible state of the world is painted in the most lively colors; a comment on which we have in the actions, conversations, contracts, quarrels and friendships of worldly men." Yes, their Actions are opposed to the law of God; their Conversations shallow, simulous, and false; their Contracts forced, interested, and deceitful; their Quarrels puerile, ridiculous, and ferocious; and their Friendships hollow, insincere, capricious, and fickle: - all, all the effect of their lying in the arms of the wicked one; for thus they become instinct with his own spirit: and because they are of their father the devil, therefore his lusts they will do.
entries.dfd9e9c7c1b5079521c5da9e0ebf8f84d4f6c537: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen55313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55314" type="x-p"/> We know that the Son of God is come - In the flesh, and has made his soul an offering for sin; and hath given us an understanding - a more eminent degree of light than we ever enjoyed before; for as he lay in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him unto us; and he hath besides given us a spiritual understanding, that we may know him who is true, even the True God, and get eternal life from him through his Son, In whom we are by faith, as the branches in the vine, deriving all our knowledge, light, life, love, and fruitfulness from him. And it is through this revelation of Jesus that we know the ever blessed and glorious Trinity; and the Trinity, Father, Word, and Holy Ghost, in the eternal, undivided unity of the ineffable Godhead.
